speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: RIGHT HON. L. S. ST. LAURENT-BIRTHDAY FELICITATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust the house will permit me to rise for the purpose of referring to the anniversary of the birth of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, former prime minister of Canada. I express on behalf of the government, and I know on behalf of members in all parts of the house, our sincere congratulations to him coupled with the wish that many more birthdays will be his.
I have known Mr. St. Laurent for more than 30 years, beginning in the days when he was an officer of the Canadian Bar Association. I was a member of the council of the bar association at that time. Later when he came to the House of Commons as minister of justice in the days of war, I followed him from time to time in debate as opposition spokesman.
During that long period, while naturally there were disagreements resulting from the holding of different political opinions, there was always that attitude of mind on his part which recognized two sides to every question. That, of course, is the essence of parliament and the strength of the parliamentary system.
Once more I express warmest felicitations and all good wishes for him today.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: RIGHT HON. L. S. ST. LAURENT-BIRTHDAY FELICITATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house of course are pleased to associate ourselves with the warm and generous tribute the Prime Minister has paid to one who I think is the only living prime minister in our country-

maintopic: RIGHT HON. L. S. ST. LAURENT-BIRTHDAY FELICITATIONS
speechtext: Oh, Oh.

maintopic: RIGHT HON. L. S. ST. LAURENT-BIRTHDAY FELICITATIONS
speechtext:
-or rather who is of course the only living ex prime minister of our country. We hope to correct that situation before long. He was also, of course, for many years the leader of our party.
We do appreciate the very gracious and generous way in which the Prime Minister has expressed what I know are the feelings of all hon. members of the house for the services Mr. St. Laurent has rendered to Canada. Perhaps I may quote one sentence
from what was said about Mr. St. Laurent this morning in an editorial in the Montreal Gazette:
It is, even more, the very special respect that must always belong to one who has so well exemplified the saying of the 18th century statesman, Edmund Burke: "Let us so conduct ourselves as patriots as not to forget that we ought also to be gentlemen".
Mr. Speaker, Mr. St. Laurent was a dedicated patriot and a strong party man, and always a respected gentleman.

maintopic: RIGHT HON. L. S. ST. LAURENT-BIRTHDAY FELICITATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this group were delighted to hear the Prime Minister graciously recognize the birthday anniversary of a distinguished Canadian. I think it is very fortunate that our democratic system and the principles and practices under which it operates make it possible for us on these and similar occasions to sheath our political daggers momentarily and recognize the service that any person has performed for Canada, regardless of their party affiliation or their views in other directions.
We heartily associate ourselves with the tribute paid by the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition, and wish the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent many happy years ahead.

A question was asked on March 2, 1960, concerning the wind tunnel construction. Two questions and the answers to them can be found on page 1642 of Hansard for that date. I do not think there is any need to repeat those answers now.
With regard to the Auditor General's report I might point out to the house that the need for a supersonic wind tunnel to do basic research in aerodynamics was discussed in 1954, and executive authority was obtained to go ahead with the plan. The preliminary estimated figure as to the cost was set at $3,750,000. The finest example of procrastination on the part of a government occurred at that time, because nothing further happened until February, 1957, when the government of the day made a firm decision to build the wind tunnel. It then took the best part of a year and a half for the design work to be carried out, and the first contract for the wind tunnel was let late in 1958. Ninety per cent of the contracts were let during the fiscal year 1958-59, and the cost estimate of $9 million was approved in June, 1959.
The Arrow was flying before the contracts for the research tunnel were let. Therefore this tunnel would have made very little contribution to the development program of the CF-105.

This is not a new tax, but the regular provincial sales tax. I intend to be quite brief, Mr. Chairman, but I rise to support this item because it does provide some measure of welcome employment to those who obtain that temporary and short term employment. From the point of view of members of this group it completely fails to meet the problem. It is a palliative, a short run approach to the question.
Before proceeding, I do want to say I appreciate the courtesy of the minister in informing the members as to the details of the regulations with respect to this program and the works that will be undertaken in the particular ridings. I also say that in my experience the municipal authorities, that is the people who very frequently work on a voluntary basis, have done their best to co-operate with the federal government in giving effect to this program. However, unfortunately the minister, with the best of intentions, is placed in the position of having to use what we consider obsolete methods to meet the present serious and continuing problem so far as unemployment is concerned.
Now, we do not blame individuals. However, it is the function of this government to try to make capitalism serve the needs of the people to the best of its ability. That is its function because it supports this present economic order, and supports so-called free enterprise. As a matter of fact, legitimate, responsible free enterprise is disappearing from the scene in many sections of industry and business. This program is an attempt to overcome the effects of planning for profits instead of planning for the welfare of persons.
This government, and all governments of the same political philosophy, recognize that the world has changed. Many years ago these unemployed persons would have been unfortunate enough to remain unemployed, without assistance. But governments have changed their views in our lifetime. The doctrine that governments must do something, even those governments supporting capitalism, to overcome the hardships occasioned by slumps or depression, is orthodox economics and entirely within the framework of the economic philosophy that this government accepts. Therefore it is trying to do something with this program.

The hon. gentleman has much more knowledge of what is legitimate or illegitimate than I have. Therefore I am unable to understand or answer that question.
As I have said, the government is trying to do something. The government tries to do all it can without trespassing on the privileges of those vested interests that more and more control our economy. That is the basic reason as we see it, Mr. Chairman, for these piecemeal, partial, part time remedies that are put forward to assist certain persons in agriculture and certain persons in Canada who are unemployed. What happens today is that these vested interests, representing monopoly capitalism, accept no responsibility for the welfare of the nation as a whole or their own employees if they have to be employed at a loss or even at a lowering of the profit rate. They leave their casualties to be dealt with by the government.
What is the position in Canada today? I understand we have between 400,000 and 500,000 persons unemployed, while at the same time we can spend over 1600 million upon armaments and so-called defence. Even reading today's newspapers we must all be conscious of the fact that there is a terrific amount of waste in that quarter. A previous speaker made reference to waste in respect of gasoline which amounted to some $144,600. That is just one of the few items mentioned in press reports of waste discovered by the Auditor General in the department of defence. I am not blaming any particular individual, but even though we are spending these huge sums of money, were it considered necessary to spend another $200 million or $300 million on Bomarc sites we would provide the money without question.
Only yesterday we learned of a United States implement corporation buying out the interest of the Cockshutt company, and because that corporation does not accept any responsibility to the Canadian nation as a whole it at once lays off many Canadian employees. It does that instead of accepting some responsibility which might entail the company operating at a loss or at a lower profit margin for a period of time. AMENDMENTS REVISING MEDIATION AND CONCILIATION PROCESSES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-5, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is one of those designed to assist the government in reducing its quota of unkept promises from 12 to 11. I am sure that in that regard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and others will find no hesitancy in supporting it. The bill is rather lengthy and perhaps I can, in the few minutes allotted to me, attempt to give a succinct but full explanation of the thoughts behind it.
Briefly, the collective bargaining process which exists at the moment by virtue of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is as follows: The two parties, that is the union and management, bargain collectively with each other directly. If no satisfactory or mutually acceptable agreement is reached by that system, the next stage is for the appointment of a conciliation officer who is an officer of the Department of Labour. He confers with the parties in an attempt to get them to reach a satisfactory solution of their differences. If the conciliation officer is not able to effect a settlement, the matter is referred to a conciliation board which consists of a representative of the union, a representative of management or the company and a person classified as impartial as the chairman, either by agreement of the two parties or by appointment of the minister without their agreement. Following upon this, if there is no agreement reached, a strike or lockout may take place. There are, of course, many other social and economic difficulties arising from that situation.
The bill before the house seeks to make some rather major alterations in that particular system which I have just outlined and which has been in effect in Canada for a number of years. I believe the system was initially established by virtue of P.C. 1003,
Industrial Relations
an order in council made during the war and applying to the entire nation. The various pieces of provincial legislation dealing with this matter grew out of that order in council and are almost parallel to this act. One of the changes sought to be made is to extend from two months to three months that period of time before which the collective agreement expires and negotiations may be opened. The thought is that the greater the length of time spent in bargaining before the actual expiry date of the collective agreement, the better the chance that some mutual agreement will be reached before the actual expiry date. Another ancillary part of that is the reduction from 20 to 10 as the maximum number of days which must elapse before collective bargaining starts following notice by one or other of the parties.
One of the major principles contained in the bill is the elimination of the conciliation board step in the negotiations, to give to the conciliation officer the powers and authorities which a conciliation board has under the act and to extend the conciliation officer's initial period of time from 10 days to 30. This gives the conciliation officer the power and authority of a conciliation board and more time in which to attempt to bring about a settlement between the parties. A new provision in here is the establishment of a period of 21 days within which either party to the collective bargaining must indicate to the minister whether or not it intends to accept or reject the recommendations of the conciliation officer. Another principle is that no strike or lockout vote may be taken until seven days have elapsed after the conciliation officer has made his report.
Another new principle contained within this bill is a provision covering the appointment of a person called a mediator who would act in that period following the conciliation officer's report, and following the rejection by either side of the report, and following a strike or lockout vote his period of time for the operation of powers similar to the conciliation officer would be 14 days. There would be an allowance of an additional seven days before a strike or lockout could take place. The bill also provides for the acceptance of a system of negotiation differing from that set out in this bill, where such system is mutually agreeable as between the two parties and is approved by the labour relations board.
Now, I should like to deal with the reasoning behind some of these changes. Negotiations between union and management now are carried on under this act and similar provincial legislation. The present system leads to a great deal of delay and procrastination. The conciliation procedures set out in

Industrial Relations
the law have been altered over the years by union and management and, in fact, are still undergoing alteration in so far as the use of them is concerned. I know that many instances both union and management, depending on the circumstances, will use the conciliation procedures contained in this act, not for the purpose of collectively bargaining in good faith but for the purpose of delay. I know of instances where union and management depending on the circumstances, will virtually refuse to make any concession or come to any agreement at the first stage of negotiations hoping when they get before a conciliation officer they may get a better understanding of the position of the other party. Likewise there is delay and procrastination before the conciliation officer and a refusal to bargain in good faith in the hope of getting before a conciliation board and the hope that the board will make a report which will be beneficial to one or the other.
Again, in negotiations which may take place before the conciliation board there may be relatively little give and take. We find that when this approach is used to collective bargaining, as it has been used in a number of instances, all the parties are doing is spending the 60 or 70 day period allowed in the act in consolidating their position, building up their relative forces and, in effect, delaying themselves into a condition where a strike or a lockout becomes virtually an assured fact.
We hope, by virtue of the bill before the house, to place emphasis on collective bargaining in good faith. We hope to indicate that if we can eliminate the conciliation board step, which in many cases is superfluous and give those powers to the conciliation officer, we would eliminate one of the steps used for procrastination by the parties. Second, the report of the conciliation officer would be in the form of recommendations such as are now made by the conciliation board. A definite limit would be established as to the length of time which must elapse before the parties indicate whether or not they intend to accept or reject the report. We allow then for a strike or lockout vote. There is also an allowance for a so-called cooling-off period of approximately another three weeks at least during which time the services of a mediator may be engaged.
From past experience we feel that any conciliation officer who is worth his salt at all should be able, in a 30 day period of meeting with union and management separately and collectively, to get their points of view about the differences. If he then makes a report recommending a basis of settlement he will make a recommendation, wherever he possibly can, on some point which he

thinks is mutually acceptable, even though the parties may not have said so themselves. This is the value of a conciliation officer, conciliator or mediator-to glean from the parties those points on which they are willing to compromise. Then we allow for the strike vote, the cooling off period, and the mediator stepping into a situation the background of which has been to promote collective bargaining, a background in which the conciliation officer has the authority, power and ability to assess the merits of each case and, of his knowledge, make recommendations. Then, if those recommendations fail to provide a solution of the difficulties, in the light of that background the mediator will have a much better chance to bring about a solution of the problems before a strike takes place, rather than giving his assistance after a strike or lockout is in effect, as is the case now.
We also propose a system of collective bargaining different from that contained in the bill, where such is mutually acceptable to the two parties in negotiations, and where there is approval by the labour relations board. We say that the particular system we envisage, the system provided for at present, or any other system of collective bargaining will not apply in toto in all possible sets of negotiations which now take place.
For the sake of argument, I can say that a certain system of negotiation might be of no use at all to the railway industry. Certainly the system in existence now is of relatively little use because in past years when negotiations went on for months and months, and even stretched into years, we found the parliament^ of Canada being asked to step in and substitute our opinions and legislative decisions for the negotiations themselves.
We think, again for argument's sake, that if the railway unions and railway management sought to work out a mutually acceptable, satisfactory system of bargaining which suits that industry, they should be allowed to use that system notwithstanding the provisions in this particular act, so long as the labour board has knowledge of that system. We may find that the same thing exists in other cases, and we should think in terms of that and not of enforcing upon management and union a system of collective bargaining which may hamstring them and prevent them from reaching satisfactory solutions. What we propose is to offer them some alternative system whereby a solution can be mutually developed, a solution which is acceptable to them, which meets the needs of that industry, meets the customs of the union and management, and which will have a better chance of bringing about a collective agreement.

To sum up, we hope by the proposed amendments to the bill to place the emphasis on bargaining in good faith. We seek to ensure that good faith will be exercised to the fullest possible extent by provision for a conciliation officer, allowing for the strike vote, the cooling off period and the provision of a mediator. We believe that by such a system, or by a mutually acceptable alternative that might be reached by union and management, we can to a measurable degree cut down the long series of negotiations that take place, cut down delays in industry and the time consumed between the opening of negotiations and the signing of a final settlement.
We also think that by doing so we shall greatly reduce the area within which both union and management now operate for the purposes of delay and procrastination to meet the needs of one side or the other. By reducing that area, coupled with placing the emphasis on collective bargaining in good faith, we think we shall promote the signing of more collective agreements with less difficulty. By doing so we would help prevent the strikes and lockouts which might develop, and reduce the number of strikes and lockouts which now take place.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS REVISING MEDIATION AND CONCILIATION PROCESSES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad, Mr. Speaker, to have this opportunity to speak on the important matters raised by the hon. member for Skeena in Bill C-5, which he has just explained to his colleagues in the house.
I have read the amendments that he proposes to the provisions contained in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, studied with some care the supplementary notes which accompany his suggested amendments, and listened with attention to the explanation he has just given us. I must confess that the amendments he proposes find favour at first blush with me, but at the outset I must say I only hesitate to give the proposed amendments stronger support because I feel the house would be ill advised to cut off one of the steps in conciliation procedure without at least consultation being had by the Minister of Labour with representatives of the Canadian labour congress and with representatives of management.
It is better that the bill proposed by the hon. member be considered by the Minister of Labour. It is better that the hon. member's recommendations, and the ramifications of carrying them out, be considered by persons who are more qualified than either the hon. member, myself, or any of us here, to determine the advisability of changes such as those he suggests.
Industrial Relations
In saying that I do not mean to minimize the weight that ought to be attached to the opinion expressed by the hon. member who, down through the years, has made considerable study of the matter; but I would feel happier in confirming my own predisposition of sympathy towards what he recommends had I the benefit of knowing what they think, and of having the viewpoint of persons of the type I have described.
The purpose of the legislation now existing is directed towards conciliation procedures. The principle upon which the legislation rests was defined in a very interesting paper read by Mr. Bernard Wilson who, at the time, was assistant director of the industrial relations branch of the Department of Labour and has since become the director of that branch, to the 14th annual conference of the Canadian association of administrators of labour legislation held in Regina in 1955. He said that the principles upon which presently prevailing compulsory conciliation procedures are founded are threefold. First of all he stated:
(1)	The public should not suffer from hasty or ill considered strike or lockout action.
(2)	There should be no strike or lockout pending compulsory conciliation.
(3)	Public opinion, informed through the investigation and report of a board of conciliation, would exert an influence toward reasonableness in labour relations.
What I find significant about Bill No. C-5 and its presentation to the house by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) is that he recognizes the need for the retention of compulsory conciliation procedures but is advocating changes that would have the effect of eliminating one of the steps that up until now has formed part of those procedures. My reason for saying this is that the hon. member says, in the explanatory notes of the bill:
This bill proposes to improve the above system of collective bargaining in the belief that it is unduly time-consuming and that the stages of negotiation repeat themselves in certain aspects with the resultant tendency to promote industrial unrest. The method used is to eliminate the conciliation board and give its authority to a conciliation officer.
So that the hon. member would eliminate step No. 3 in the presently existing conciliation procedures. The fundamental principle upon which the conciliation procedures rest, as indicated by Mr. Wilson in the extract I mentioned a moment ago, is to avert the cause of a strike that would cause inconvenience and hardship to too large a number of people. The right to strike is never, surely, questioned by anyone in this house. It is true it is a powerful weapon, but it has been used on many occasions in the past in this country

Industrial Relations
and on this continent to advance the cause of the workingman, and a just strike deserves public support.
A strike, it is true, is capable of causing much hardship and much inconvenience, not only to the workers themselves who go on strike but to other persons who are not even remotely connected with the strike. One of the tests of the justice of any strike is, I suppose, the extent to which steps have been taken prior to its institution; the extent to which preliminary procedures have been exhausted and have been conducted by the parties in a spirit of good faith.
The present conciliation procedures-which are only briefly mentioned in the explanatory notes-are more thoroughly dealt with by Mr. Wilson in the paper to which I referred a moment ago. He describes the procedural stages as being four in number and says they are these:
(1) Direct negotiations by the parties. This is basically a collective bargaining procedure but is considered a conciliation stage here because it must be completed before conciliation can be requested. In my view, there is nothing to prevent the parties from being mutually conciliatory; unlike mediation, third parties need not be present.
The hon. member for Skeena does not suggest that stage No. 1 as it presently exists be eliminated. Stage No. 2, according to Mr. Wilson, is as follows:
The appointment of a conciliation officer (in nearly all provinces), upon application if direct negotiations have not resulted in agreement.
(3) The appointment of a conciliation board, if a settlement has not followed from the appointment of the conciliation officer.
It is stage No. 3 that the hon. member recommends we should eliminate. Stage No. 4 is not part of the legislation but is part of the prevailing practice. It is described by Mr. Wilson in his paper as being:
Post-conciliation board conciliation, in which industrial inquiry commissions, chief conciliation officers, deputy ministers and ministers of labour seek to bring the parties into agreement on the basis of the recommendations of the conciliation board or on any other basis possible.
Again, the amendments proposed to the existing legislation by the hon. member would not eliminate this present practice from the procedure that is followed. It is of interest, I think, to give some brief consideration to the extent to which strikes have been avoided in the past with reference to the various stages presently existing in the conciliation procedures.
I am informed that if we examine the statistical data with reference to federal projects for the fiscal year 1959-60, some 76 per cent of disputes within federal jurisdiction were settled at the conciliation officer stage of the procedures now prevailing in

the act; that is to say, a little over 75 per cent of the disputes terminated on the desk of the conciliation officer.
The figures apparently would indicate, too, that the average settlement over a period of about 11 years is 62 per cent. In 1959-60 the figures that have been made available to me would indicate that out of 91 disputes dealt with to finality in that period, 69 were settled and the remaining 22 either went before a conciliation board, lapsed or were in some other way settled.
Apropos the same branch of my subject matter, that is to say extent to which disputes have been settled with relation to the various presently existing procedure stages, Mr. Wilson in his paper had these comments to make:
To illustrate statistically, there are a great number of disputes settled by the direct collective bargaining negotiations provided for by collective agreements or by legislation. No figures are available but they would amount to all agreements signed in any period less those in dispute. Figures are available with respect to settlements in the remaining three stages of conciliation. For instance, of 46 railway disputes assigned to conciliation officers over an eight year period, 21 of them were settled without requiring boards of conciliation. Of 24 of the remaining disputes that were submitted to boards, 12 of them were settled directly by the boards. Eight of the 12 remaining disputes were settled by post-conciliation board intervention. One dispute lapsed and strike action was taken in three disputes.
It will be seen that, of 46 disputes, only 3 resulted in strikes; that it is the final result that matters and not the settlement failures along the way.
The main criticisms that we hear expressed of stage No. 3 of the present procedures, the stage which the hon. member for Skeena recommends that we should eliminate, is first of all the expense of the conduct of these conciliation boards. Then second, and perhaps just as important, is the allegation that the personnel who constitute the boards are invariably-as I read it somewhere

called partisan special pleaders whose object is not to settle the dispute at all but to have the point of view of their party to the dispute prevail with the chairman of the board, and that in the result the chairman carries on under pressures being brought to bear upon him on both sides that render any possibility of worth-while decision remote and unlikely.
I think there is a good deal of merit in many of the criticisms that are voiced about this stage of our present conciliation procedure-the expense, the partisanship of those engaged in it, though one has every sympathy with the points of view put forward by those who appear at these boards. These are factors which cause me to wonder about the advisability of retaining the conciliation board as one of the steps in the present procedure.

The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) in his explanatory note and, I think, in his comments a little while ago, said that the conciliation board procedure, prolonging as it does the over-all conduct of the procedures generally, had a tendency to create industrial unrest. I heard some criticism of that point of view; someone stated that the hon. member was making the mistake of assuming that by cutting off the procedure he was cutting off the dispute. I am not sure this is really a fair criticism of the objective of the hon. member in the presentation he has made to the house.
There are features of this bill, as I have already intimated, which commend themselves to me. I only refrain from giving them stronger support because of my desire to be given the opportunity to study the bill with the guidance of persons such as the representatives of the Canadian labour congress and of Canadian management, who are better qualified than either myself or the hon. member, in my opinion, to advise the government what kind of changes in the existing legislation would work out in the most satisfactory manner. I am not satisfied that I fully appreciate the ramifications which would follow if we were to agree without further guidance or study to the recommendations made by the hon. member, particularly with regard to the recommendation that we abolish the procedures presently provided for before the conciliation board.

Mr. Speaker, just the other day I had the opportunity in this house to make mention of the fact that one of the things which particularly blessed our young country was the fact that being a country in the new world we have avoided much of the bitterness, let us say, of the cleavage, which existed years ago between owners, workers, employers and employees in the old world. I think this is one of the remarkable and happy things which has underlined our life in Canada. This has been made possible, I feel, by the farsighted attitude of both major parties inside and outside the House of Commons in regard to labour relations. Nobody realizes better than the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) the impossibility of directing a country like Canada today sans la grande cooperation des employeurs, des employes et des gouverne-ments a tous les echelons.
I should like to say also, before getting into the details and into the pith and substance of the discussion this afternoon, that Canada has also been blessed in the main, by responsible union movements and responsible management. I think it is good that we should underline this fact in relation to Canadian 26207-1-30i
Industrial Relations
management and unions. It is something that we often take for granted, but it is something of which I feel we should, nevertheless, be most proud. The previous speaker said he thought this bill should not be passed before it is discussed in detail with representatives of management and labour. With this condition I am in full accord. I am similarly in accord with many of the proposals he placed before us for our consideration.
I do not want to place too much emphasis on my next remark, but I cannot help making it, because I think it demonstrates the fundamental difference in approach between those who sit on my right, those who support the N.D.P., and those who support this government. The hon. member made the remark that he thought a provision in this bill would help guarantee good faith. I know he was sincere in his contention, but I also know that is one of the fundamental differences between members of my party and members of his. I do not believe you can legislate for good faith.

speechtext: The hon. member must have misunderstood me or else I did not make my meaning clear. I did not say that by legislation we could guarantee good faith. What I said, or what I intended to say, was that we should place a system of negotiation into effect in which good faith would be allowed to play its full role.

speechtext: I certainly stand corrected. I know the hon. member placed his contention before the house in all sincerity. However, I re-emphasize that he and members of his party perhaps place too much emphasis on the good faith which can be created by government legislation. That, to me, is one of the errors which runs through the hon. member's whole bill, namely that by changing procedural details you can increase or decrease good faith among the parties involved.

speechtext: Again, the hon. member is not interpreting me correctly.

speechtext:
I should like to make two points. Broadly speaking, I think the sponsor of the bill is in fundamental error in his understanding of the actual provisions of the present legislation. I think he is also in fundamental error with regard to the effect which the provisions of his own bill would have on the present legislation. As the hon. member who has just spoken pointed out, although the bill only talks about three stages we have, in actual practice, four stages of conciliation. There is the stage of conciliation which can, and often does, follow the finding of the conciliation board. What the hon. member has assumed, wrongly I think,

Industrial Relations
is that many of these cases, or even a large percentage of them, go through all the stages of conciliation. I am referring to his assumption that they go through all these four stages when in point of fact they do not. A good many of these casess touching upon the federal jurisdiction are solved long before they get through the greater part of these stages. As was mentioned, and I repeat it, only a few actually do go through all four. In 1959-60 some 76 per cent of the cases in federal jurisdiction were settled by conciliation officers.
It is also much more important to look at the proceedings as a whole than to look at any step of the proceedings at any particular time.
In considering this legislation we should consider the possibility of the Department of Labour introducing amendments to the law which would give the conciliation officer a discretion as to whether or not a hearing should actually go before the conciliation board. I think this will come about before too long. This is desirable and wise.
The discussion today in my opinion has been of a useful nature but before commenting further on its value let me say this. The provincial authorities in Alberta and British Columbia have instituted action respecting conciliations along the lines of the bill presently before us and although we have no statistics on this point it is my impression that the experience in those provinces has been that strikes are not settled more quickly than in the federal field under present procedures.
Another point should be emphasized. It is one of the announced purposes of the present bill to avoid delay. I am sure it is the hope of the sponsor that any legislation arising from this bill would deal with disputes that are being stubbornly contested by actually cancelling, so to speak, one of the existing steps of procedure. I do not feel this will be helpful in reaching that objective. As was so ably pointed out by the previous speaker, the sponsor of this measure appears to feel that if we cut off the procedure we will cut off the dispute. Actually, the result will be that an increased number of disputes will lead to strike action whereas under the present act there are few strikes. It will not be of good service to labour relations if the legislation is designed so that the parties to a dispute may disagree more quickly. In fact, narrowness will be promoted rather than lessened if the bill as presently drafted becomes law.
For the purposes of general discussion of this vital subject I wish to place on the record some views about which more can be
[Mr. Grafftey.l
said for than against. I offer the following suggestions for the improvement of present procedures:
1.	Eliminate frivolous proceedings by having the parties bear the cost of conciliation as they now do arbitration.
2.	Endeavour to eliminate narrowly partisan board members by a panel arrangement chosen in advance by labour and management.
3.	Place legislative emphasis on the power of a conciliation officer to recommend against the appointment of a conciliation board in certain situations.
4.	Place a time limit in the legislation beyond which a strike or lockout might take place even if the conciliation procedures are not completed.
5.	Follow the administrative practice of avoiding or refusing post-conciliation board intervention wherever possible.
6.	Give conciliation officers and board chairmen more tactical guidance in meeting disputants separately and together, stressing with board chairmen the fact that settlements are preferable to recommendations.
7.	Develop board chairmen in greater numbers and from all professions. As part of their development, provide them periodically with a wide range of reading material in labour relations.
8.	Present periodically an organized and spirited exposition of the values of prevailing conciliation procedures, in order to offset biased or unjustified criticism.
As I indicated earlier, I advance these points for general discussion and consideration. I would be the last to say that in a field so vast as that of labour relations each of these proposals has been implemented but I feel any fair minded, objective member of this house would agree that under the guidance of the Minister of Labour we have made great advances in relation to the points I have just outlined. I'would agree that much still remains to be done and I have mentioned the desirability and possibility of the Department of Labour introducing amendments to the existing act which would have the effect of altering the role played by conciliation officers.
I do not feel it would be wise to pass the bill now before us without first calling in for consultation representatives of management and labour as was proposed by the speaker who preceded me. We must consider the fact that the sponsor of this measure is attempting to legislate with respect to good faith by introducing procedural changes. I differ with him in respect of his view that this measure will achieve the desired result through eliminating one of the steps of the process. I again remind hon. members of the

experience in those provinces that have incorporated this idea in terms of settling strikes as compared with the experience in the federal field under present practices.

For the reasons I have outlined I must oppose this bill. I am able to say, however, that the points of view introduced by those hon. members who have participated in the debate have been helpful.
At the outset of my remarks I commented that we in Canada should be proud of our experience in the field of labour relations. Modern developments and improved methods should be reflected in our legislation. It is of importance today that legislation of the type under discussion should be modernized and kept abreast of the times. We in the new world realize the importance of co-operation between management and labour and all levels of government. Bipartisan discussion such as we have had this afternoon assists us in reaching this goal. I do not for a moment feel that we disagree about the desirability of achieving the aims sought to be achieved by this bill but I believe there does exist a sincere and definite disagreement concerning the procedural methods by which to achieve the desired end. speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I am quite opposed to closure. I shall curtail my remarks so that the house may take a decision on the bill.
Labour relations are largely a provincial responsibility. It is true that the federal responsibilty in this field embraces an area which involves a relatively small proportion of the total number of workers in Canada. However, that is not the test of the importance of federal labour legislation. It seems to me that federal labour legislation has an importance far beyond that number of employees whom it directly concerns and that it
Industrial Relations
must, in my view at least set the example for good labour legislation in the country.
When the 1948 legislation was passed I for one had high hopes that sections 62 and 63 of that act would find favour with the provinces and that the legislation would prove to be of such value that the provinces would seek to avail themselves of opportunities given under those two sections. However, 1 have been somewhat disappointed in that respect. Perhaps the provinces are right in relying on their own legislation. At the moment I am not passing judgment on that matter or expressing an opinion on it.
The history of this legislation is rather interesting. The 1907 act, which was the forerunner of the present act, was in relation to its time a model of legislation. It became out of date and was not amended perhaps as quickly as it should have been amended. Then in the war years the orders in council on this subject represented distinct steps forward. They were good in relation to their times and the circumstances of their times. The 1948 bill which is now the existing act was an excellent improvement.
For my part, I should like to see this legislation closely examined again so that it could be updated in order to meet the requirements of the present day. The rapidity of technological development in the field of industry has placed on management-labour relations strains that were not in existence a few years ago. Yet in this last decade since that development has taken place we have not kept pace with it and have not kept our legislation in line with the added requirements; we simply have not modernized it as it should be modernized. To the extent that the hon. member in this legislation has sought to modernize the legislation to meet that kind of changed requirement, I think it is wholly desirable. For my part I should like to have the opportunity of going through the bill in a detailed way, as is proper in committee, in order to develop those views more fully.
Over the years, when labour matters have come up for discussion, it seems to me that the debates in the House of Commons on this subject have tended to support either one point of view or another as to labour or management and that in doing so hon. members have perhaps tended to ignore the role of government in this field and not to devote enough attention and argument to the question of how government could improve the legislation in order to make sure that it was the most perfect legislation that it was possible to draft for the purpose of meeting the existing needs.

Industrial Relations
Sometimes when I hear some of my colleagues speak in the House of Commons and when I read of the exhortations of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to management or to labour, I wonder whether they have forgotten the role of government in this field. I refer to the role of government in perfecting the legislation. One of the things that is needed at the present time is speedier conciliation and an examination of our present processes for conciliation which in principle are very good and in which I as a Liberal member of the House of Commons with knowledge of the history of this act can take some pride. However, they should be examined and should be modernized.
I am not clear as to why the sponsor of this bill seeks to remove the conciliation board and to replace it by a mediator. I can well understand that process being applied as to a large segment of industry but I cannot understand it in all cases. As far as I am concerned, there is requirement for clarification on that point. For my part I should like to see the conciliation board retained in a slightly more precise or clear form than is indicated. The mere substitution of a mediator is something which I do not think accomplishes the purpose the hon. member is seeking to accomplish. However, to the extent that it does so, and with the changed time limits he proposes, it would make for speedier conciliation in a large sector of the field it occupies.
At the outset of my remarks I said that I would not speak until six o'clock but that I would give the house an opportunity of taking a decision on this matter. I therefore because of the time resume my seat.

speechtext:
I wish to deal with the item under consideration as objectively as possible. I intend, of course, to deal with it in the light of the serious problem it is supposed to solve.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, before asking ourselves whether or not this winter works program can be effective in view of our serious unemployment situation, we must determine exactly what situation the program is supposed to cope with.
I should like to read again into Hansard the figures which were first issued by the dominion bureau of statistics to the effect that there were 349,000 unemployed in Canada as at November 30, and 413,000 at the end of December.
I have said previously in this house that D.B.S. figures are necessarily rough figures only because they are not based on complete sampling.
The minister will recall that I wrote to him around December 15 to enquire how many unemployed were drawing unemployment insurance benefits as of November 30.
(Text):
I wish now to thank the minister for his prompt reply. This letter is dated December 21, 1961 and is addressed to me by the Minister of Labour. It reads as follows:
The information which you sought in your letter of December 15 regarding persons drawing unemployment insurance benefit is as follows:
Active claimants as at November 30, 1961
Atlantic	 49,168
Quebec	 107,561
Ontario	 115,429
Prairie	 61,285
Pacific	 52,521
Total	 385,964
Now, if we compare this figure of 385,964 with the figure released by the dominion bureau of statistics of 349,000 for the end of November, we come to the conclusion that the figure released by the bureau of statistics is surely incomplete. I should like an explanation from the minister. No doubt, he will be able to reply to my question at the end of this debate.
Supply-Labour
On January 29, as reported on page 293 of Hansard the hon. member for St. Henry asked the following question:
According to the most recent statistics, how many unemployed are in receipt of unemployment benefits?
The answer given by the parliamentary secretary to the minister was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, a record is not available at any given time indicating the number of persons actually in receipt of benefit since payments are made at varying intervals in the case of postal claimants and personal payments at local offices.
At the end of this debate, Mr. Chairman, I should like the minister to explain why it was not possible to give the hon. member for St. Henry the number of unemployed drawing unemployment benefits at the end of December when it was possible to give those figures to me on December 21. I should like also to ask the minister, from now on, around the 20th of each month when he gives us the figures from the dominion bureau of statistics, to give us the figures for unemployed persons drawing benefits so that we will have a more complete picture of the situation.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, the figures I gave a moment ago show clearly what the situation is. It is serious, because of all its implications, for the families of those unemployed workers.
We can now wonder what is the government's stand on this issue, not only on the problem that has confronted us for four years, but the one we face today. The government is again submitting to us the only measure directly meant to solve the unemployment problem, namely the winter works program.
The first complaint I have to make about the government stems from the very item submitted by the minister for our approval; indeed this measure put before us today deals with seasonal unemployment only.
This government has never recognized the national and urgent character of the unemployment problem we have lived with these last four years.
Apparently, the only remedy the government knows is the winter works program. I shall say later what I think of the principle of that program. However, I want to point out that since its inception about four years ago, it has not been expanded enough to meet the problem which has become more and more serious.
I have studied the annual report of the Minister of Labour, particularly the one submitted for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1961. I want to be fair. I want to give here figures that indicate the scope of that program.

Supply-Labour
First, during the period I have just mentioned, I notice that 2,162 municipalities took advantage of it. Yet, if I remember rightly, there are at least 4,000 municipalities in Canada. I must admit that the largest municipalities took advantage of that program, but I am sure that, had it been made more attractive, a greater number would have participated therein.
I note here that those projects have provided employment for 120,816 persons and that the average employment was for approximately 45 man days. As for the average wages, I think they are a little under $200 per person although I did not calculate them exactly.
I note that the over-all estimated cost of the projects undertaken adds up to $212 million, while the federal contribution in wages adds up to $36 million. That means that the federal contribution to all those projects does not exceed 17 per cent. I think we may conclude here that a nation-wide program was introduced but that the federal government does not assume the share it should and that we let the provinces and municipalities carry most of the load.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I shall concede that these results I mentioned a moment ago are better than nothing, but the government will never convince the Canadian people, and particularly those who are out of work, that it is with such a program that we shall reduce unemployment, especially when it is as heavy as it is now.
However, I am prepared to admit one thing. During the past few years, I have tried to think of all kinds of solutions which could help to reduce unemployment. Among the short term solutions, I still do not know of any program which could bring faster results that the one involving projects undertaken jointly by the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
But if we are to deal efficiently with unemployment, we have to widen the scope of this program, and here I have a few suggestions to make. First of all, I shall endorse some suggestions which were submitted yesterday by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).
In the first place, the scope of those projects should be broadened so as to interest almost all the municipalities in this country, where unemployment prevails.
Second, I think that the federal government should shoulder a larger proportion of the cost of salaries. You know that the government contributes 50 per cent of the payroll costs, and I may point out that the province of Quebec adds to those 50 per cent
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
a sum equal to 40 per cent, which represents in all 90 per cent of the payroll costs, so that the municipality needs only contribute 10 per cent, in addition to the cost of materials.
We also know that six other provinces are adding 25 per cent to the federal contribution; accordingly, I imagine that, if the latter, in an all-out offensive, would for instance, decide to contribute 75 per cent of the payroll costs, which might mean an additional expense of $25 million at the most, the municipalities would be able to go ahead in this field, and get much more positive results than we have now.
Here is another suggestion, Mr. Chairman. During a period of national emergency like the one we are now going through with regard to unemployment, the government should consider the possibility of paying part of the cost of materials and of the supervising personnel.
A special fund for loans at a low rate of interest should also be put at the disposal of the municipalities where unemployment is more acute.
The sales tax on materials used during the winter works program could also be reduced, or eliminated. All those steps would be of assistance to the municipalities.
When a high level of unemployment lasts for several years, as is the case at present, and particularly in the areas which are most affected, I also believe that the government should consider the opportunity of extending this program several months a year and, if necessary, to cover the entire year. Such a policy would be in accordance with the recommendation made by the municipalities in May of last year according to a report published by the Star in its May 2, 1961 issue, I believe. I quote:
(Text):
The resolution asked that the program be extended to cover the entire year on a "make work" basis, with the federal government contributing 50 per cent of the total costs involved for such work from June 1 to October 15.
It asked that during the rest of the year the federal government contribute 75 per cent of the total costs of the winter works program and make prompt interim payments and early final settlement.
The resolution also asked that the federal government provide loans to municipalities for winter works at a reasonable rate of interest-
-and so forth.
(Translation):
However, Mr. Chairman, before adopting such a broad program, there should be, at the

government level, a meeting of the federal Minister of Labour and the various ministers of labour of the provinces, in order that strong action might be taken in an effort to alleviate the situation from which too many of our Canadian families are suffering.
I think the government should remember one thing, which is that Canadians are sick and tired of the half measures taken by this government. I believe that this winter works program, which is being submitted to us again this year, while basically sound, is nothing else but a half measure which does not attack the heart of the problem.
Mr. Chairman, I think there is no other conclusion to draw than the following: we have a winter works program designed to alleviate seasonal unemployment, while what we need is a large scale, exceptional program designed to fight unemployment, which of course is more than seasonal in character.
It has been said and repeated-and the highest authorities have said so-that our citizens were entitled to work, and in this regard may I be allowed to quote what His Eminence Cardinal Leger stated, in a lecture, as reported by Le Droit of September 18, 1958:
A society is not sound if it does not provide for each one of its members the possibility of living humanly from the fruits of his labour.
The right to work is a natural right. It corresponds to the duty we all have of working to earn our living.
Mr. Chairman, when a danger of war threatens, all the forces of the nation are mobilized to safeguard national security. For four years, we have felt the gnawing symptoms of a non seasonal ailment, and once more, hundreds of thousands of our fellow Canadians are now suffering hardship; I am of the opinion that if we mobilized forthwith all the forces of the nation, we could implement a far-reaching program which could not only reduce unemployment but almost completely solve the problem.
If in war time we mobilize the whole nation, we certainly must be willing to pay the cost of such mobilization. The same applies to our unemployment problem. If we want to find jobs for most of the Canadians who are now unemployed, we will have to foot the bill.
For four years, this administration has given evidence that it is prepared to go only half way in this direction. The Liberal party is prepared to pay the full cost necessary to give jobs to the unemployed of this country.

That, of course, is the official position taken now but, on the contrary, these were not the recommendations of the opposition; they were the recommendations and the requests of the Canadian municipalities who from time to time review this program with us and make suggestions. We implement those which come within the scope of the program and, as a matter of

fact, we have widened the scope of the scheme to an extent which most hon. members will recognize. In spite of all the criticism and all the debunking of this program in which the opposition has been indulging during the past four years, the municipalities have disregarded that attitude. They look upon this as being a very successful and helpful program and consequently they are participating in it to the extent which I have indicated.
I wish, now, to turn to Hansard and deal with some of the remarks which were made yesterday in this debate. The hon. member for Essex East, referring to figures on unemployment issued by the dominion bureau of statistics and released on or about the middle of each month with respect to the previous month, said:
Normally we would have received that figure-
-he was referring to a figure for January 31-
-some time around the 20th of the month.
That point has no substance at all, because the figures which are released by the D.B.S. refer to a sampling taken in the middle of the previous month. The hon. member went on to say:
Perhaps before this debate is over the minister might explain why we have not received it as yet.
Well, the hon. member for Essex East- and I am sorry he is not here today-knows very well, because he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of labour that these figures are not released until the date when they are supposed to be released, and that this date ranges anywhere between the 18th and 24th of the month. The hon. member said I could easily have given the committee an interim report, but there is no interim report at all. This just goes to show the type of argument to which the official opposition is indulging-arguments not based on facts of any sort.
The hon. member for Peterborough made a few remarks yesterday, and among other things he said, as reported on page 412:
I am sure all of us are extremely happy to find that the percentage of unemployed has been going down.
At any rate that is an admission. Then the hon. member went on:
This does not result from anything this government has done. They have no reason to take any credit for this fact.
Well, I am prepared to prove to the committee that this reduction in unemployment is directly attributable to the measures we have put into effect over the past number of years. The hon. member went on to say:
After all, it was only last winter that this government said you could not do anything about unemployment.

I intend to go into detail on that aspect of the subject to prove that this government has recognized unemployment and the importance of dealing with it ever since we took office on June 21,	1957. Then the hon.
member went on to say:
Management and labour must sit down together, but who is going to provide the opportunity?
May I remind the committee that we called a meeting upon the insistence of those who said the same thing not too long ago. We called together 15 of the leading industrialists of this country representing various important manufacturing industries. We called in 15 top labour leaders and we said: we have brought you together; let us see if you can settle your differences and thus help the economy. But there has not been another meeting-

We did call one. These are grown men, men holding positions of responsibility in the economy of this country. Not only that, but since then they have formed joint committees including the president of the Canadian labour congress and the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for the purpose of determining when another meeting should be held. We called these people together. We did our duty because it was insisted that we should have the original meeting. I do not know what the hon. member for Peterborough thought these people would be doing. Possibly he thought they would be advising the government on economic problems. Far from it. This meeting was called so that the leading men in industry and labour might be able to settle some of their difficulties in order that the economy might be capable of rapid progress in the future.
The hon. member for Peterborough went on to say:
What is wrong with this program is the fact, of course, that it is completely and utterly inadequate for the kind of unemployment that Canada is facing and will face.
Of course, this particular program does not represent all that we are doing. It is just one of the programs that we are introducing, representing some $40 million of expenditure, in order to look after a certain section of our unemployed by reducing the seasonal unemployment with which we are faced during the winter months. The hon. member said later:
What about technological unemployment?
What are we going to do about that?
Has the hon. member not heard what we are doing about that? Has he not heard that we are building some 167 schools across this country to take care of this very problem?

The hon. member talks about planning. We are building for the future of our young people. Is that not planning?

We get another winter works program. That Is all this government can do-
Mr. Chairman, I intend to spend some time telling the hon. member just what the government is doing, because he is apparently not aware of what is being done; if he is aware of what the government is doing, then he is not telling the facts to the people of this country.
The hon. member for Welland in the course of his remarks attributed to me the statement that unemployment would melt away with the snow. I have never said that. I have been one of those who have resolutely stood by this problem, because I realize the hardship people have to go through when they find themselves out of employment. I have endeavoured to do everything within the capacity and the power of this government to bring about a better situation for these people. To say I have done so is another example of the disregard for the facts in which the opposition has indulged in the course of this debate.

My fourth criticism, and most serious charge against the winter works program, is that it misleads the people of this nation into believing that this is all that a federal government can do, that this is the sum total of the federal government's duty to deal with the national problem of unemployment.
That is quite untrue, Mr. Chairman. That is not the sum total and this government did not give that indication. This is but one measure. This is one phase of what we are doing.
