At this very moment hundreds of municipalities that have participated in this program are awaiting the passing of this item so that they may receive cheques of which they are sorely in need to pay their accounts in respect of this work.
Hon. members of the official opposition speak as though recession had commenced in 1957. Apparently they have forgotten what happened in 1954 and 1955. It might be well to remind them of the remarks made by the present Prime Minister at that time speaking in the debate on unemployment in 1955. If the government of that day saw fit in 1955 to allow a debate on unemployment, surely there must have been a substantial degree of unemployment to justify that debate.
The present Prime Minister as reported at page 2035 of Hansard of March 15, 1955 used the following words which I feel are worth repeating at this time:
We do not believe in preaching pessimism; we do not want to see the condition of affairs brought about which will create panic; but we are asking the government to act now-
The Prime Minister on that occasion made it clear that we in the Conservative party do not believe in preaching pessimism. He said we did not want to see those conditions and asked the government to act immediately.

In the few brief lines I have quoted from the remarks of the Prime Minister in 1955 is summarized the difference in attitude between the present opposition and members of this party when we were in opposition. We do not believe in preaching panic and pessimism. Obviously hon. members of the opposition do believe in preaching panic and pessimism because they feel it is the only way they can influence the Canadian people and get back into office. I do not believe the Canadian people are gullible enough to be influenced by this false attitude. Panic and pessimism appear to have become the cornerstone of the policy of the Liberal party at this time. Hon. members of that party have no other policy.
In 1955 we asked the government of that day to act. The fact is that the government at that time took no action whatever. The government was not interested in unemployment. Hon. members of the government of that day took the attitude that unemployment was none of their business. Their approach was simply to create a climate in which prosperity could be maintained. Unfortunately, however, they did not succeed in that endeavour, either.
When in 1955 the present Prime Minister asked the government to act, 7.7 per cent of the labour force in Canada was unemployed. Unemployment levels were much higher than they are at this moment. When members of this party in the opposition of that day asked the government to put forward some measure under which municipalities could participate in projects to alleviate the situation the then minister of labour, as reported at page 1608 of Hansard of March 1, 1955 said, in effect, "There is no way at all by which the federal government can or should go over the heads of the provinces and deal directly with the municipalities."
This was another enunciation of that great Liberal principle "it can't be done". Mr. Chairman, we have made a success of the program which we asked the Liberals to implement. We did it. We have proved it can be done. I repeat that at that time 7.7 per cent of the Canadian labour force was unemployed.
"We must look at the situation in a calm and dispassionate way." That was the statement of the minister of labour in 1955. The Liberals now say they have all the answers. If you examine the Liberal answers closely they embrace everything that the Conservative government is now doing, item for item. The Liberals now pledge that they are going to educate people in technology and institute municipal winter works programs, but always

bigger and better than anything we are doing. That is the policy upon which they are building their election plans.
Hon. members of the opposition now say that the recession began in 1957. That is their stand. I wonder how they described conditions in 1955. Mr. Walter Gordon is now playing a very important part in planning the affairs of the Liberal party. According to the report of the royal commission on which he served there was a slowing down in the economy as far back as 1949. The Liberals were saved at that time by increasing United States buying which resulted from the Marshall plan and by the increase in defence commitments resulting from the Korean war. In 1954 the recession really set in, in earnest, and they did nothing about it.
Even in the face of mounting recession they kept the economic brakes on. The Liberals did not discover unemployment until 1958 when they found themselves out of office after being in power for 22 years. They were not aware of unemployment in 1954 and 1955 and that, I wish to stress, is when the cycle began. It began in 1954 and continued in 1955. In 1956 there was a shortlived pickup largely on account of increased investments. This had run its course by the summer of 1957 when we took office.
The charge has been made that this government has failed to recognize unemployment. No doubt it was in the course of our failure to recognize unemployment that we called a national conference on unemployment in July 1958. From that conference emerged a number of measures, among them the municipal winter works incentive program. No doubt it must have been in the course of our failure to recognize unemployment that we broadened the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We raised the number of weeks during which people could receive benefits from 36 to 52, introduced amendments relating to married women and men, brought fishermen under the act and made it easier to obtain seasonal benefits. We lengthened that period by an additional two months. It must have been in that action that we failed to recognize unemployment.
No doubt it was also because we failed to recognize unemployment that we embarked upon the most massive program of public housing in Canada's history.
It must have been our failure to recognize unemployment that brought about the special session of parliament in November 1960 for the purpose of bringing forward additional measures to deal with that problem. I might comment also that the performance put forward by the opposition during that session
Supply-Labour
so far as concrete recommendations is concerned was rather pitiful. The government, on the other hand, brought forward some 25 measures designed to stimulate the economy and provide jobs for Canadians. I submit that this is how we failed to recognize unemployment. These are the charges we are hearing today. The actual fact is that from the time we took office we made it clear that we recognized unemployment and that we were prepared to use all the means at our disposal to put Canadians back to work. Already in the summer of 1957, when we took office the signs were there. When we took office unemployment was increasing at an ominous rate. Vast wheat surpluses were piled up on the prairies and the former government told the western farmers there was nothing they could do about it. That matter also has been dealt with by this government. Tight money was in full force at that time-there is no question about that matter-put into effect by the then Liberal government. The former government was still fighting inflation long after any danger from that quarter was over. As a matter of fact, they are still fighting inflation.
I am struck by the qualms expressed by the opposition with regard to the budgetary deficit of the present government. I wish to point out to hon. members that the accumulated wartime deficit of the former government was well over $10 billion. Apparently it could be done in wartime but, in their opinion, it cannot be done in peacetime when the objective is to put Canadians back to work and to get the economy rolling in high gear again. And they call us the party of big business.
Opposition speakers in this debate have not dwelt to any extent on the manpower situation. Perhaps the reason is that in December unemployment was the lowest in five years in terms of the labour force. In this connection I should like to refer to an article of date of January 8, written by Mr. Patrick Nicholson who is a representative of the Thomson papers in the press gallery. Mr. Nicholson said this:
In the past four years more than half a million workers have been added to Canada's labour force. Jobs have been found for a staggering 430,000 of these up to November last. In contrast, during the postwar conversion period between 1946 and 1950, only 334,000 were added to our work force and only 310,000 new jobs were created, despite the great consumer spending spree of those years.
In contrast again, during the four years 1951 to 1955 which included the Korean armaments boom, only 267,000 new jobs were created in all Canada.
Those are the remarks of Mr. Patrick Nicholson. Mr. Nicholson adds that the past four years have been our best ones since the war when measured by that important yardstick of the number of new jobs created for Canadian workers.

Supply-Labour
In December 1961, with a labor force totalling approximately 6,500,000 Canadians, more than 6 million Canadians were gainfully employed or 93.6 per cent of the labour force. This meant an increase in the number of persons working of some 465,000 over the figure for December 1956 or practically half a million more.
I wish to make this point as it seems somehow to have escaped the attention of the opposition or at least they are reluctant to talk about it. We have put a great many people to work. The measures put forward by this government have been to a great extent instrumental in reversing the recessionary trend. The solutions which this government has brought forward are those for which they voted in this House of Commons. As I mentioned earlier, they voted for every one of them. Every one of them was not any good, according to them but they voted for them. However they are the measures they are now bitterly attacking.
I well recall Mr. Walter Gordon's announcing on television-I was present on the program-that the most effective solution to our problems would be the devaluation of the dollar. He repeated that statement time after time all during the whole program. I doubt whether he said anything else. He told us that we had only to do this and that everything else would follow. We did it. Mr. Gordon's friends are now criticizing this measure. This is the gentleman who is directing the whole Liberal program. He took over from the hon. member for Essex East. He is evolving the whole Liberal social plan and policy. Now the Liberal party are criticizing what Mr. Gordon said was the only thing to do. Mr. Gordon himself has now come out in favour of a municipal works program. I say to you Mr. Chairman, that Mr. Gordon is just about four years too late. I wish to say this, that a program which could put into motion some $760 million for municipal projects over a four year period is no mere bagatelle, regardless of what the hon. member for Essex East wishes to call it or whether the hon. member for Assiniboia calls it peanuts.
Mr. Gordon and his friends are also saying that perhaps we should embark on a training program in order to upgrade the labour force. They do not seem to be aware of the 167 new schools we are building across Canada or of the facilities we are providing for some 80,000 students at a cost of some $270 million, of which the federal contribution already approved totals some $141 million. I submit that this in itself is quite a program of public works which is going on right at this moment

and is providing jobs for people in the construction industry. Perhaps they consider this program to be a bagatelle also. This government has brought into motion and into effective and positive action, a program striking forward on all fronts of economic activity, a program to stimulate the economy and to provide jobs.
We know what would have happened had the situation remained as it was in 1954 and 1955 and had the government adopted the attitude that was adopted then. Had we adopted that attitude the spokesmen for the opposition would have had reason to cry havoc around the country at this time. They would have had something to cry about. Where were the "bold and imaginative" programs when they held office? Where now are the "bold and imaginative" solutions? The boldness and the imagination have been demonstrated on this side of the house during the time we have held power. As I mentioned earlier, they were unable to offer any help to the municipalities. They always said, "It can't be done" and this was their standard answer. There were no concessions for the provinces. It could not be done. They were not prepared to evolve a massive training program to meet present needs. These training programs should have been started many years ago in order to take care of what is happening now to our labour force because of automation and technological changes.
Slum clearance, grants to assist in maintaining our water resources, the opening of the northland, a national oil policy, aid to exporters, aid to small business, tackling the wheat surplus, freeing Canadian enterprise from outside domination, aid to underdeveloped regions, housing on a massive scale such as that implemented by this government-all these achievements were beyond the initiative of those whose policy was based on the principle of standing pat and not rocking the boat.
This government has tackled all these problems. It has tackled every single one of them. It has tackled the problem of unemployment right from the beginning from July, 1957. I do not pretend that all the problems are solved, Mr. Chairman; far from it. However, very positive and active progress has been made.
Indeed, in the midst of preachments of doom and depression, Canadians have retained confidence in their economy and in their country. I want to refer to a recent Gallup poll, Mr. Chairman, which shows that 45 per cent of Canadians are convinced that the standard of living in this country will continue to rise. I assume also that that 45 per cent relates to those who have confidence

in the policies of this government. There are 6 per cent who feel that our standard of living will go down, according to the Gallup findings. Undoubtedly, Mr. Chairman, they have been listening to the opposition members, to the N.D.P. and Liberal members such as the hon. member for Essex East and the Leader of the Opposition. There are 46 per cent who are convinced our standard of living will not go down. Presumably they, too, have confidence in this government's policies.
In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I should like to put on the record a portion of a front page article which appeared in the Financial Post of December 23. I quote:
We have passed from discouraging recession to bright new growth in business activity-The promise now in the economy is a clear broadening of expansion on the base of recovery established in 1961. GNP might top the $39 billion mark for a 6 per cent gain over 1961. So it will be a good year for most firms, a remarkable year for the shrewd few and, for all, perhaps the best chance of doing business since 1956-
The article adds that unemployment remains a problem, which we admit at once, Mr. Chairman, and at all times. Then, the article continues:
But it would be nonsense to pretend that the federal government has not pushed the process to the advantage of all Canadians by a number of commendable actions.
Amongst those commendable actions, Mr. Chairman, the Financial Post lists first, the devaluation of the dollar; second, the export drive and, third, monetary management. This could hardly be called fulsome praise, but it is at least an admission that this government has taken certain steps which have proven helpful to the general economy. I say we can take credit for that. If we have to take responsibility and abuse for something that has not been done, then when something is done I say we have every right to take credit for it.
In that respect, I submit also that this stand compares favourably with the opposition stand that none of the measures for which they voted were measures appropriate to the situation. I might add also that the pessimism portrayed by the opposition has not found echo in the daily press except that part which is the die-hard Liberal press and supports the Liberal party.
These were some of the headlines appearing on December 22 following the third quarter release on national production by the dominion bureau of statistics. The headline in the Ottawa Citizen reads:
Canada gets glad tidings on economy.
Mr. Charles Lynch of the Southam news service went on to say this:
Supply-Labour
In almost every sector of the economy except agriculture, things were humming at such a pace during the third quarter of this year that the gross national product rose by 2.7 per cent, the largest quarter to quarter advance in several years- Labour income reflected the largest increase since 1959-
The headline in the Toronto Globe and Mail reads:
Production jumps record 2.7 per cent in third quarter.
Shaking out the last effects of recession, the Canadian economy leaped forward to establish records between July and September-
I did not write this, Mr. Chairman. This article was written by Mr. Bruce MacDonald in the Globe and Mail. The Canadian Press reported the economy as moving ahead strongly, and attributed the improvement to rising consumer and government spending. I assume, Mr. Chairman, that hon. gentlemen opposite also read the newspapers but do not pay any attention to them. In one breath they say we have done nothing, and in the next breath they say we have done too much.
We invested, Mr. Chairman, in the municipalities. We invested in the provinces to the extent that the increase in federal contributions to the provinces, by itself, would have cancelled our deficits and would have shown a modest surplus. We invested in the young people of Canada with the largest training program in history. We invested in schools. We invested in universities. We invested in sewage disposal. We invested in urban redevelopment. We invested in the small businessman through the expansion of the industrial development bank. We invested in Canadian research and Canadian export, in the farmer, in the aged, in the war veteran and in the great resources of our northland.
Let us see what the situation is now. The unemployment figure for December was the lowest for any December in five years. Is this cause for complacency? Certainly not, there is no cause for complacency, although one recalls this phrase from Mr. Gordon's royal commission report:
In a free and dynamic economy in which people are entitled to change their occupations as they choose and to move from place to place and in which there are continually changing products, methods, and consumer demands, there will always be those who are out of work at any given time. This cannot be avoided. It helps to keep the economy flexible-
This is the same Mr. Gordon who says now "We can give full employment." This government believes in keeping people at work. I would point out that average employment in the third quarter was 3 per cent above last year. Non-agricultural employment on the average was 3.6 per cent above last year and the number of men working in the third quarter was 2.9 per cent higher than last year. Manufacturing production in the third

Supply-Labour
quarter was 5 per cent over the first quarter. Employment in manufacturing industries was
83.000	higher than a year earlier. There were
83.000	new jobs, Mr. Chairman, in manufacturing alone. This is certainly a very welcome improvement.
Employment in the electrical apparatus industry in the fourth quarter, for example, was 7 per cent above a year earlier. Employment in primary iron and steel was up 4 per cent. In shipbuilding, employment was up 20 per cent over last year. I ask hon. members opposite, do they really think that a 20 per cent increase in the number of people working in the shipyards is merely an accident? Do they not think this was the result of action taken by the government, that it had something to do with the subsidies announced by my colleague, the Minister of Transport? The hon. member for Peterborough says that we should not take any credit for these things. I say to you that this is something for which we should take credit because we took action in this regard. This is an example of another investment in Canada and in Canadians.
Two recent developments in the manpower situation are also worthy of note. There were fewer women coming into the labour force and this is related to the fact that more men are working. There were 125,000 more men working this year than last year. There are fewer young people coming into the labour force, with a consequent increase in school enrolment. They are staying in school to complete their education. Finally, in December, there were 180,000 more people at work and 115,000 fewer people out of work. There is evidence that increased economic activity is being translated into more jobs and fewer unemployed.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this government has moved all along the line to correct situations which were in evidence when we took office. These situations were in evidence, as I said earlier, as early as 1954 and 1955. Amongst the problems in evidence at that time were tight money, a wheat surplus, growing unemployment, dropping exports, uncertainty in industry, a labour force where new skills and training were badly needed, with municipalities, the provinces and labour unable to get a hearing at Ottawa.
Since we assumed office we have moved against these problems with positive and effective programs designed to meet the developing situation, and the results of these programs are now beginning to appear. Many of the economic anomalies are now being corrected, with the result that in spite of world wide competition the economy is once again on the upswing. At the same time we have not neglected social measures such as

care for the aged, the blind, the handicapped, the war veterans and many others.
Now, in the process of meeting these objectives deficits have occurred but may I say that never in the history of social and economic reconstruction have budgetary deficits accrued for more worth-while reasons than those incurred by the present government. The work we are doing in the labour field, the up-grading of the labour force with the aid of the winter works program in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities, the stepping up of production through cooperation of labour and management in the productivity council are objectives which we shall continue to pursue and these, along with many other measures in the government's economic program, will provide a stimulus to the economy and employment for men and women in Canada.
The situation in the latter part of 1961 has been increasingly hopeful. The upward trend in economic activity, which resumed in the second quarter, has gained momentum as the year progressed. In the third quarter the gross national product, seasonally adjusted, increased by 2.7 per cent and this was the largest quarter-to-quarter advance in several years.
It is also worth noting, Mr. Chairman, that this gain was almost wholly accounted for by an increase in physical volume of output. Prices remained stable during the quarter and in this connection I would refer to the Montreal Gazette annual commercial review and forecast, published on January 13. The leading article is headed as follows "Upswing reflects rising physical volume". The subheading reads:
Extremely easy monetary policy is causing no forebodings while devalued dollar stimulates domestic production.
In that sentence is summarized the twin aspects of monetary policy which is proving both beneficial and stimulating to the economy at the present time. I shall just quote one sentence from the article which follows:
For the first time in post-war history, the economy was launched upon a period of growth without the usual accompaniment of price inflation.
I would point out that the third quarter gain in output raised the physical volume of production to a level 3 per cent above the first quarter of 1960. In the goods-producing industries the quickening tempo of expansion led to increased output of 3.5 per cent in the third quarter. The strong expansion which has been marked in the service industries continued in evidence at a slightly diminished rate of 1.5 per cent. The rise in goods-producing industries is particularly encouraging because this has been one of the soft spots in every economic downturn.

Particularly large gains were recorded in the motor vehicle industry, which I am sure will be a source of satisfaction to a great many people in my riding of Ontario and in those of the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Essex South, because employment in that industry is up by 6 per cent.
Another encouraging factor has been the increase in consumer spending in the last half of 1961. The average increase for the first nine months was 4 per cent higher than in the corresponding period of 1960. A number of figures have already been placed on the record by my colleagues in the debate on the speech from the throne, but I feel some of them bear repetition if only as an indication of the results that have been achieved. For example, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has placed on record the tremendous increases in exports, and I would suggest that an increase of $160 million in wheat sales is a matter for encouragement. An increase of $33 million in sales of nickel is also cause for a certain degree of satisfaction, as all these sales find their way back into the Canadian consuming stream, add to the purchasing power of the nation and, in the end, mean more jobs.
Construction employment and farm employment have both kept up at a time when a seasonal decrease is to be expected. Thus, from the figures I have mentioned and from others which have been placed on the record by my colleagues, it is evident that the outlook is good for employment this winter. A continuation of the current upward trend would mean the provision of new jobs for some 200,000 Canadians.
I have already mentioned the notable improvement in manufacturing. The value of manufacturers' shipments in November was up 7 per cent over the previous year and gains were registered in every province. In automobile production, while employment was up 6 per cent, output increased by 20 per cent between the fourth quarter of 1960 and 1961.
Average output in steel production was 25 per cent above a year earlier and employment was up 5 per cent. Perhaps this is what is meant by a falling off in production, as described by the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the N.D.P. Another encouraging factor has been the sharp increase in domestic production of cotton fabrics, reversing the downward trend of several years ago in the textile industry.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in analysing all these changes there can be little doubt that steps taken in the fiscal, monetary and income transfer fields by the federal government have contributed to the improvement in the
Supply-Labour
economy, and we can take credit for that with a great deal of satisfaction.
The actions that this government has taken were an important factor in stopping the developing downward trends in evidence during the past several years before they had time to develop into a major recession. In order to do this we have had to enlist the support of provincial and municipal governments, and of both management and labour through such organizations as the productivity council. I may say that in by far the majority of cases this support has been forthcoming, and thus we have had the spectacle of the federal government working hand in hand with the many important elements in the community in order to provide that leadership which was so urgently needed.
We have not been afraid to accept suggestions and advice from various groups, such as business and labour as well as provincial and municipal bodies. We have checked this advice against the reports we have received and the results have been positive and beneficial.
When people talk about economic planning, when they talk about socialism and say socialism means economic planning, I ask this question: are not all these measures which the government has introduced, are they not all in the category of economic planning in a free enterprise, democratic country, not the strait-jacket type of action in which people are regimented.
Surely one can realize that these things did not just come about without planning and advice from the best economists this country could produce and the advice of the other bodies which I have mentioned. But that, I submit, is the great difference between our type of planning in a free democracy and the type of planning in socialism that the hon. member for Peterborough suggests. The practical effect of the programs we have undertaken is shown in such examples as the approval of more than $100 million in assets for double depreciation by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This means the establishment of new industries and new jobs in areas where such industries and jobs are needed. These are not theories; these are facts.
As the impact of government action becomes more fully evident in the economy there will take place an added expansion and impetus as a result of that action. By direct federal government expenditures, by expenditures directed to the provinces and municipalities, the spending level of all governments has been raised by 6 per cent in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961. Federal investment has taken up the slack left by a drop in private investment.

Supply-Labour
My hon. friends opposite will agree, I am sure, that this is a course recommended by every serious economist in Canada and the United States for a condition such as we found in 1957.
At the present time private investment is picking up and as inventories grow and plant expansion proceeds it can be expected that government spending will moderate accordingly. This government has evolved a program that is putting new life into the economic bloodstream of this country. Other and complementary measures will be required from time to time to complete this program and the program of national development to which this government and the Conservative party are committed. This we have done and will continue to do.
In five years recession has been rolled back, new jobs have been provided, stimulus has been injected into the economy, vast social and economic measures have been brought forward. The Canadian people sought leadership in 1957 and 1958 and that leadership has been forthcoming in the person of our Prime Minister and his government, who have given tremendous leadership to this country, who have put tremendous life into the veins of this country and its economic forward movement. I say in conclusion, Mr, Chairman, that the record speaks for itself.

We have lived up to the recommendations of that committee.

It is obvious. It is because the government realizes that a deficit is valuable. That is obvious. That is what we have been saying. These means may certainly be used, but they must be planned so that you can put more purchasing power, more cash into the economy in order to achieve a healthy response. You certainly do not try to cut off the money supply and then end up with an unexpected deficit and talk about having done so in order to create employment. That is the kind of backward thinking of which this government has given so many examples in the past. Obviously this government does not realize that changes of emphasis are needed from time to time-that you only sail a ship by constantly adjusting the wheel.

This government does not make any adjustment until the whole economy has practically gone down the drain. Then, finally, they come to the realization that deficits were needed in the first place. There is one thing I notice about these schemes: nearly every one of them was put through during the last session beginning last November.

The Minister of Labour suggested that a special session was called last November to deal with unemployment, but I seem to remember that the speech from the throne last November did not even mention the word "unemployment". Turning back to the numbers game which the minister has been playing, it is interesting to note the suggestion made not too long ago that 115,000 more people are employed this year than were employed last year. I wonder how many of them can really be regarded as occupying productive jobs created by this government. We increased the armed forces by 15,000; we put 25,000 into survival training for six weeks. We have another 12,000 in training. Probably the imposition of sales tax in Ontario has put a few more people to work. When you get down to it you get about 60,000-about half as many as it has been suggested are now in productive employment in this country as a result of steps taken by this government.
The minister talks about vocational schools. Yes, I know that the answer, one of the answers to unemployment given by this government, was to throw a lot of money at the provinces and say: here is a vocational training program. But it was not a vocational training program; it was a school building program, and in order that we might get some people at work building the schools the government decided that they should all be put up by 1963. Thus there was no time to find out what kind or size the communities concerned needed. There was no chance to plan a program. What the provinces did was to put up as many buildings as they could and then hope they could find enough courses of instruction to make the whole thing worth while, together with students who would fit into those courses.

them to accept them, as one would expect- they realize it would cost them less to provide tor a school in the county itself than it would to continue to send students to the municipality. Thus the municipality is now in the position of losing students to the county. In some cases this system may even be impairing the movement toward the integration of education which was taking place in parts of Ontario. We have students who were being brought into larger school units now attending classes in vocational schools set up in rural areas.

Under our constitution education comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces but I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that vocational training is not a matter of culture, language or religion. The federal government should assist in this field and give direction and purpose. Only the federal government can provide leadership. Only the federal government has statistics and the other information required. As it is now, money is pumped in and the period given for construction is too short to accomplish an intelligent result.
I refer the minister to the efforts of the Ontario industrial education council. The minister must know about what I am saying now because people in his constituency are active in this area. It provides full consultation among educational bodies, school boards and management from various industries concerning the type of school to be constructed and the type of vocational training that could best supplement the industries in a given area. I am always interested in numbers. Perhaps the minister will explain the following aspect of his program which I have never understood. Perhaps it was explained before I arrived in this chamber. The program is based on a 27-28 week basis. The municipality receives a contribution of 50 per cent of wages in relation to those employed on municipal works approved by the federal government over a 27 or 28 week period. When it comes to calculating how many are employed the basis is brought down to 9 weeks. In order to proceed on a logical basis surely you should assume that it is one job per period of the winter works program, that is one job for a 27 or 28 week period.
The figure showing those employed under the program for 1958-59 instead of being

Supply-Labour
41,500 should have been about 13,000. The figure for 1959-60 instead of being 51,600 should have been about 17,000. The figure for 1960-61 instead of being 121,000 should have been about 40,000. The figure for 1961-62 instead of being 111,100 should have been about 41,000.
The federal government pays $1 or $2 per $10 paid by the municipality. The amount of employment attributable to the federal percentage of the payment for 1958-59 should be 2,000 men and the figure for 1961-62 should be 8,000 men. That is the result when you bring it right down to exactly what the federal government is doing over a period that the program is in operation. I do not understand the reference to a nine week period. I do not know of any place in Canada where the winter lasts only nine weeks except possibly Victoria and Vancouver. Perhaps the minister can enlighten me as to why in order to produce larger numbers, a nine week period is assumed in totalling the number of people who are being employed under the program.
The minister told us about many measures which have been implemented. What about the things that were not done? From the minister's remarks one might gather that we had full employment in Canada, that everything is fine.

Mr. Chairman, I was just as shocked as you and my fellow members were to hear a teacher squarely oppose the vocational training program introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for the benefit of the coming generation. I was, moreover, very much surprised and shocked to see that a teacher could afford the luxury of awarding school boards, and more particularly those of

his riding, a certificate of incompetence, stating that they did not know what they were doing nor where they were going.
For a school teacher, who wants to promote education and training, it is certainly an astounding attitude which he will certainly regret one of these days.
I wanted to draw the attention of this house to that statement and to point out to the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman), that he has jumped feet first into a tight spot from which he will find it very difficult to extricate himself, come the election.
Mr. Chairman, we are now discussing the estimates of the Minister of Labour, one of which relates to the winter works program.
For the record, I want to make a few remarks concerning the projects which this program brought about, not only throughout Canada and the province of Quebec but, more particularly, in the constituency I have the honour to represent here, that is, St. Hyacinth e-Bagot.
According to a report published by the municipal authorities of St. Hyacinthe, five municipalities in that riding availed themselves of the program inaugurated by the Minister of Labour during the fiscal year 1960-61.
For instance, the city of St. Hyacinthe has undertaken works amounting to a total of $71,511, which represented $35,962 in labour, and which provided jobs to 146 persons.
The municipality of St. Joseph, which is adjacent to the city of St. Hyacinthe has, for its part, undertaken works amounting to a total of $6,600 which represented $6,330 in salaries and jobs for six persons.
The village of La Providence has also undertaken works amounting to $16,000, which included $10,500 for labour, and this provided work to 15 heads of family.
The municipality of St. Damase has undertaken $13,902 worth of works, $5,235 of which went to pay wages to 30 heads of families.
As for St. Nazaire d'Acton, it spent $800 to provide work for ten people and pay them $690 in wages.
Two hundred and seven of my fellow citizens found employment on those projects for which $57,917 were paid for labour expenses.
